target.title: Inferring imagined speech using EEG signals: a new approach using Riemannian manifold features

read.pdf: Figs. 1–9 and Tables 1–4 visually checked in the publisher PDF; all 16 pages, including references, read

entries.text: The authors propose imagined-speech classification using covariance-matrix descriptors on a Riemannian manifold, tangent-vector features, and a relevance vector machine.
entries.condition: EEG; classification of closed-set imagined vowels and words.
entries.quote: A novel method based on covariance matrix descriptors, which lie in Riemannian manifold, and the relevance vector machines classifier is proposed.

entries.text: The authors claim that the method outperforms approaches in the field in accuracy and robustness; the reported evaluation primarily measures accuracy and κ.
entries.condition: Comparisons use this study's speech-imagery dataset; robustness is asserted but no separate robustness metric is defined.
entries.quote: The method is shown to outperform other approaches in the field with respect to accuracy and robustness.

entries.text: The authors claim this is the first report examining conditions that affect imagined-speech classification.
entries.condition: Novelty claim about comparisons across sound, meaning, and word complexity.

entries.text: The authors state that the 15-subject imagined-speech EEG dataset is published and provide a Dropbox link.
entries.condition: The linked dataset is the study's collected imagined-speech data; no code or model weights are said to accompany it.
entries.quote: The dataset of speech imagery collected from total 15 subjects is also published.

entries.text: The closed label sets are vowels /a/, /i/, /u/; short words in, out, up; long words cooperate, independent; and short-versus-long in versus cooperate.
entries.value: 3 vowel labels; 3 short-word labels; 2 long-word labels; 2 short/long labels
entries.condition: Subjects imagine internal pronunciation without overt vocalization or muscle movement; the short-versus-long task uses only in and cooperate.

entries.text: The cohort is 15 healthy adults (11 male, 4 female; ages 22–32); all are right-handed except S13. Subjects completed one to three task-specific sessions, each about 1 h.
entries.value: 15; 11 male; 4 female; ages 22–32; 1–3 sessions per subject
entries.condition: The per-task cohorts differ; Table 2 reports 8 vowel subjects, 6 short-word subjects, 6 long-word subjects, and 6 short-versus-long subjects.
entries.quote: Each subject performed one to three sessions of imagined speech.

entries.text: Each task session presents 100 randomly ordered trials per word or sound; a visual cue identifies the target, with repeated beeps pacing covert pronunciation and an approximately 2 s rest between trials.
entries.value: 100 trials per label; approximately 2 s rest
entries.condition: Short-word and vowel rhythm period T=1 s; long-word and short-versus-long period T=1.4 s. The visual cue lasts 7T; the beep sounds at trial start and four more times.

entries.text: The analyzed interval is intended to contain the visual cue after auditory cues have stopped, to avoid classifying beep-evoked activity; the authors classify labels at the same rhythm.
entries.condition: Beep rhythm is a task pacing cue; the analyzed segment is described as visual-cue-only, not a different-rhythm classification task.

entries.text: EEG was recorded with a BrainProducts ActiCHamp and 64 electrodes in the international 10/20 system, at 1000 Hz and then downsampled to 256 Hz.
entries.unit: electrodes; Hz acquisition; Hz after downsampling
entries.condition: Scalp EEG from healthy adult participants during the task protocol in Sec. 4.1.

entries.text: Preprocessing applies a 5th-order Butterworth 8–70 Hz band-pass, a 60 Hz notch, and an electro-oculogram artifact-removal algorithm.
entries.unit: filter order; Hz passband; Hz notch
entries.condition: Applied to the recorded EEG before CSP, covariance features, and classification.

entries.text: CSP selects spatial channels; binary CSP is used in most cases, multi-class CSP occasionally in short-versus-long classification, and component count is chosen empirically per subject and test condition.
entries.condition: The paper does not identify whether CSP fitting and empirical component selection are confined to each training fold; see unstated entry t58.

entries.text: The primary low-level feature is the CSP-filtered EEG; the optional second stream concatenates channel index, raw signal, and Morlet-wavelet features, then uses PCA for the short-versus-long task.
entries.value: 8 octaves; 10 voices; 80 scales; retained scales 8–40; 35-dimensional low-level vector; PCA to 15–30 components
entries.condition: Frequency features did not improve vowels, short words, or long words; method 2 combines tangent vectors from spatial and wavelet covariance matrices for short versus long.

entries.text: Covariance matrices are mapped to tangent vectors using the geometric mean computed from training covariance matrices; that training reference is then used to normalize the dataset.
entries.condition: The paper explicitly gives training-set geometric-mean tangent normalization; it does not report whether additional per-feature z-scoring is enabled in the linked mRVM implementation (see t65).

entries.text: A multiclass mRVM with multiple Gaussian kernels classifies tangent features; the typical kernel parameters are listed but are adjusted by subject and case.
entries.condition: The manuscript does not report the exact adjustments or identify which mRVM1/mRVM2 implementation variant was run; see t68.

entries.text: The decoder assigns a class label and the RVM formulation provides a class-membership confidence; the task output is one of the cued phoneme or word labels.
entries.condition: Closed-set classification; no continuous transcription output is evaluated.

entries.text: Main proposed-method results use randomized 10-fold cross-validation. Three-class vowels and short words use 270 training and 30 test trials; two-class long words and short-versus-long use 160 training and 40 test trials.
entries.unit: folds; training/test trials per task set
entries.condition: Each class has 100 randomly ordered trials per session; splits are described as random, with group-specific participant cohorts listed in Table 2.
entries.quote: To evaluate the proposed method, we performed a 10-fold cross-validation procedure.

entries.text: Short-word and vowel trials use a 4 s analysis window, split into three 2 s epochs with 1 s overlap; long-word and short-versus-long trials use 4.5 s, split into three 2 s epochs with 1.25 s overlap.
entries.condition: Short/vowel window comprises expected speech imagery plus 1 s after cue disappearance; long-task windows are per trial.
entries.quote: For short words and vowels, we extracted 4 s for each trial.

entries.text: The abstract reports a maximum 70% accuracy for three-word classification; Fig. 8 presents per-subject means and ranges, with the three-short-word group using in/out/up.
entries.condition: Three-class short words in/out/up; subject-level 10-fold random CV, 90%/10% split (270/30 trials); Fig. 8 displays per-subject min/max, and the abstract does not name the maximizing subject.
entries.quote: The classification results of all cases are presented in figure 8 and table 1, which show the mean, minimum and maximum values for each subject participating in each group.

entries.text: The abstract reports a maximum 95% accuracy for a two-word case; Fig. 8/Table 3 show this as the short-versus-long method-2 maximum for S14 (in versus cooperate).
entries.condition: Two classes, short word in versus long word cooperate; method 2 combines spatial and Morlet-wavelet features; S14; 10-fold random CV with 80%/20% split (160/40 trials).
entries.quote: The classification results of all cases are presented in figure 8 and table 1, which show the mean, minimum and maximum values for each subject participating in each group.

entries.text: Mean of the per-subject mean accuracies for vowel classification is 49.0 ± 2.4%.
entries.condition: Three classes /a/, /i/, /u/; participants S4, S5, S8, S9, S11, S12, S13, S15 (n=8); per-subject 10-fold random CV, 270 train/30 test trials; Table 2 averages subject means and standard deviations.

entries.text: Mean of the per-subject mean accuracies for two long words is 66.2 ± 4.8%.

entries.condition: Two classes cooperate/independent; participants S2, S3, S6, S7, S9, S11 (n=6); per-subject 10-fold random CV, 160 train/40 test trials.

entries.condition: Two classes, in versus cooperate; method 1 uses spatial features only; participants S1, S5, S8, S9, S10, S14 (n=6); per-subject 10-fold random CV, 160 train/40 test trials.

entries.condition: Two classes, in versus cooperate; spatial features only; participants S1, S5, S8, S9, S10, S14 (n=6); per-subject 10-fold random CV, 160 train/40 test trials.

entries.text: Mean of the per-subject mean accuracies for short-versus-long method 2 is 80.1 ± 8.0%.
entries.condition: Two classes, in versus cooperate; method 2 concatenates spatial and wavelet tangent features; participants S1, S5, S8, S9, S10, S14 (n=6); per-subject 10-fold random CV, 160 train/40 test trials.

entries.condition: Two classes, in versus cooperate; method 2 concatenates spatial and wavelet tangent features; participants S1, S5, S8, S9, S10, S14 (n=6); per-subject 10-fold random CV, 160 train/40 test trials.

entries.text: Chance level is 33% for three classes and 50% for two classes (Fig. 8); the text defines C%=50% explicitly for two classes.
entries.condition: Applies to the three-class vowel/short-word tasks and two-class long-word/short-versus-long tasks, respectively.
entries.quote: where P% is the prediction accuracy, and C% is the chance level, i.e. C% = 50% for two classes.

entries.text: The authors state that the averaged accuracies across task groups are above chance.
entries.condition: Task-group means in Table 2; chance is 33% for three classes and 50% for two classes (t30).

entries.text: The paper calls all accuracies significantly above chance but does not report a statistical test against chance; Table 4 tests methods against each other.
entries.condition: No chance-level null test, confidence interval, or chance-test p-value is reported for the 10-fold results.
entries.quote: which is well above chance level.

entries.text: For vowels, the authors report RVM 49.0 ± 2.4% versus ELM 45.2 ± 2.3%, paired t(7)=3.48, p=0.01.
entries.condition: Three vowel classes; 8 subjects; comparison of the mean accuracies reported for Table 3(a).
entries.quote: the RVM (µ = 49.0, σ = 2.4) performed better than the ELM classifier (µ = 45.2, σ = 2.3 );

entries.text: For short words, RVM 50.1 ± 3.5% versus ELM 46.6 ± 4.2%, paired t(5)=3.26, p=0.02.
entries.condition: Three short-word classes in/out/up; 6 subjects; comparison of the mean accuracies reported for Table 3(b).
entries.quote: the RVM (µ = 50.1, σ = 3.5) also outperformed the ELM classifier (µ = 46.6, σ = 4.2 );

entries.text: For short versus long words, RVM 73.3 ± 8.9% versus ELM 76.3 ± 5.8%; paired t(5)=1.39, p=0.16, described as equivalent.
entries.condition: Two classes, in versus cooperate; 6 subjects; the prose comparison concerns the reported spatial method-1 short-versus-long averages.
entries.quote: the performance of the RVM (µ = 73.3, σ = 8.9 ) and the ELM classifier (µ = 76.3, σ = 5.8) was quite equivalent;

entries.text: The authors say combining the spatial and wavelet feature streams improves short-versus-long classification in most subjects; Table 2's group mean rises from 73.3% to 80.1% (t26, t28).
entries.condition: Short word in versus long word cooperate; method 2 concatenates tangent vectors from spatial and wavelet covariance matrices.

entries.text: Similar performance on three short words and three vowels is interpreted by the authors as evidence that sound, rather than meaning, supports discrimination.
entries.condition: Comparison is between the three-class /a/, /i/, /u/ task and the three-class in/out/up task, with different subject subsets in Table 2.
entries.quote: based on the sound rather than the meaning.

entries.text: The authors infer that longer, more complex words are more easily discriminated, based on the long-word versus short-word and short-versus-long comparisons.
entries.condition: Long-word group is cooperate/independent; short-word group is in/out/up; the binary comparison is in versus cooperate.
entries.quote: Thus, words with higher complexity can be more easily discriminated using EEG signals.

entries.text: A reconstructed block-ordered vowel experiment yielded 99.3 ± 1.4% accuracy (minimum 96.7%, maximum 100%).
entries.condition: One subject S8; vowels /a/, /i/, /u/ imagined 55 times consecutively per section; 5 blocks × 11 imagery trials per vowel; 50 two-second epochs per vowel after 1 s overlap; MultiCSP plus tangent features and RVM or ELM; 10-fold cross-validation with 20% evaluation (10 test samples per class).
entries.quote: The accuracy was (99.3 + / −1.4)% with min 96.7% and max 100%, using 10 cross validations and 20% evaluation, i.e. 10 testing samples for each class.

entries.text: The authors say the block-ordered protocol creates temporal correlation and makes its very high accuracy erroneously optimistic; this is a deliberately reconstructed protocol, not the main randomized task.
entries.condition: Reconstruction involved one subject and three vowels; see t46. The authors contrast blocked repetition with randomly ordered trials.
entries.quote: the high recognition rate is erroneously optimistic.

entries.text: The authors acknowledge that RVM training is computationally expensive because its optimization is non-convex, even though they consider testing speed more important.
entries.condition: General mRVM training limitation; no training-time measurements are reported for the study.

entries.text: The authors note that tangent-vector flattening may not fully preserve nonlinear discrimination of the original SPD manifold, while describing it as more computationally efficient and nearly equivalent to other distances.
entries.condition: Riemannian covariance/tangent representation used for the reported EEG tasks.

entries.text: The authors state that Riemannian feature computation is more expensive than Euclidean features and that covariance matrices can be singular or semi-positive-definite with few samples; CSP is their feature-selection mitigation.
entries.condition: Limitation of covariance-matrix descriptors and eigenvalue-decomposition distances.

entries.text: The authors report that tangent-feature ELM results can be unstable with large standard deviation, plausibly because ELM randomly chooses first-layer weights; they prefer the more stable RVM.
entries.condition: Observed in the study's ELM-versus-RVM comparisons on vowel, short-word, and short-versus-long data.
entries.quote: The result of RVM is more stable, and hence preferred in our approach.

entries.text: In their Hurst/ERICA implementation, subject S13 retained only 33, 23, and 28 useful trials for the three vowels; the authors regard such rejection as too restrictive for robust training and real-time use.
entries.unit: retained trials per vowel; trials available per class
entries.condition: S13; vowel classes; Hurst exponent threshold 0.70–0.76 and ERICA independent-component rejection in the authors' implementation of a prior method.

entries.text: The authors caution that their lower results when applying DaSalla et al.'s procedure may reflect different instructions: that study involved vocalizing/mouthing vowels, whereas this study emphasized sound imagery.
entries.condition: Comparison is a reimplementation on this paper's dataset, not a direct comparison of published test-set numbers.
entries.quote: In contrast, our experiment emphasizes on imagery of the sound, which is more related to speech imagery.

entries.text: The authors describe speech imagery as consistent across users and easier to perform and repeat without initial training, motivating it as a BCI input.
entries.condition: General framing from related work; the present study's analysis is per-subject and does not evaluate novice training or deployment.

entries.text: The manuscript gives random partitions and 10-fold CV but does not report the random seed, independent repetitions of the full CV, or fold-to-fold split variability beyond summary statistics.
entries.condition: Main proposed-method results in Sec. 5.2; linked generic code also omits an explicit RNG seed (t63–t64).

entries.text: No held-out-subject or cross-speaker evaluation is reported; results are tabulated separately for individual subjects, with trials randomly partitioned within task datasets.
entries.condition: Per-task cohorts differ (n=6–8 of 15); the paper does not test transfer to unseen speakers or subjects.

entries.text: The paper does not specify whether CSP fitting, component-count selection, subject/case kernel adjustments, and PCA-dimension choice were determined strictly within each training fold or using independent validation data.
entries.condition: CSP counts are chosen empirically; mRVM parameters receive small subject/case adjustments; no nested or separate selection-set procedure is described.
entries.quote: The number of CSP components was chosen empirically and it varied between 6 and 14 depending on the subjects and testing conditions.

entries.text: The paper segments each trial into three overlapping epochs but does not state how the proposed RVM combines epoch predictions into a single trial-level decision.
entries.condition: Short/vowel trials: 3 × 2 s epochs with 1 s overlap; long/short-versus-long trials: 3 × 2 s with 1.25 s overlap. Explicit voting procedures are described for comparator methods, not for the proposed method.

entries.text: Beyond the stated training-set geometric-mean tangent normalization, the manuscript does not state whether per-feature centering/scaling or the linked mRVM code's optional standardization flag was enabled.
entries.condition: This uncertainty concerns additional z-scoring of feature dimensions, not the explicitly described Riemannian reference-point normalization.

entries.text: The paper describes class-label decoding by mRVM but does not describe an external language model, lexical prior, or post-decoding language constraint.
entries.condition: Closed vocabulary of prompted phonemes/words; no continuous speech transcription task.

entries.text: The reported evaluation is offline cross-validation; no live, closed-loop BCI deployment, online adaptation, or user confirmation/correction study is described.
entries.condition: The conclusion frames combining imagined speech with other modalities as future work.

entries.text: The linked repository's generic cv_mRVM2_MKL script makes one randperm(N) permutation and assigns contiguous permutation chunks to folds; no explicit RNG seed appears in that script. The paper does not identify this exact script as its runner.
entries.condition: Repository-level implementation detail only; paper reports random 10-fold CV but does not confirm the repository CV wrapper was used.

entries.text: The linked mRVM2 multi-kernel training script initializes auxiliary Y with rand and W with randn, with no explicit RNG seed in that function; the manuscript gives no initialization or seed setting.
entries.condition: Repository implementation detail; the paper does not identify mRVM2_MKL as the exact variant used.

entries.text: The linked training wrapper exposes optional per-feature standardization; when enabled, standardize_data computes mean and standard deviation from the training fold, replaces zero standard deviations by 10e-6, and the prediction script reuses those stored values. The manuscript does not say whether the option was enabled.
entries.unit: replacement standard deviation for zero-variance features
entries.condition: The wrapper receives X_train_cv for training; no inference is possible about the flag used in this paper from the generic repository alone.

entries.text: The linked mRVM training and prediction wrappers use build_standarized_kernel, which divides each cross-kernel entry by the square root of its corresponding training/test self-kernel diagonals; the manuscript does not describe this kernel normalization.
entries.condition: Generic repository implementation; the exact script variant used by the paper is not specified.

entries.text: The linked prediction script evaluates multinomial-probit class probabilities using fixed 2-point Gauss-Hermite quadrature and then normalizes probabilities across classes; the manuscript gives the expectation but not this numerical approximation.
entries.condition: Repository prediction implementation; no confirmation that this exact helper or setting was used for the paper's reported results.

entries.text: The manuscript refers to multiclass mRVM from references 29–30 but does not identify the exact mRVM1 or mRVM2 variant; the linked repository contains both variants and their multi-kernel forms.
entries.condition: No result can be assigned to a specific repository variant without an experiment-specific script or parameter record.
entries.loc: Sec. 3.1.4; linked mRVM repository README and training scripts

entries.text: The imagined-vowel labels were /a/, /e/, /i/, /o/, and /u/; a mute, zero-volume sound was also used as a control condition.
entries.condition: Vocabulary: five Korean vowel syllables plus mute; EEG-based imagined speech; decoding/LM and seeds not reported.

entries.text: Cohort: five healthy male native Korean participants, ages 26–32 (mean age 28.25 ± 2.71); participants were right-handed and had normal hearing.
entries.condition: Subjects/speakers: five healthy males, native Korean, right-handed; the paper reports per-subject results and no held-out-speaker split.

entries.text: Participants heard the cues and imagined the target for 3 s; each syllable was tested in five sessions of 10 trials (50 trials per vowel and mute condition).
entries.condition: Vocabulary: /a/, /e/, /i/, /o/, /u/, and mute; auditory cue followed by imagined speech; no decoding/LM or seeds reported.

entries.text: EEG was resampled to 250 Hz, filtered at 1–100 Hz with a 59–61 Hz notch; the 3-s imagery period was split into 30 0.2-s segments with 0.1-s overlap. Mean, variance, standard deviation, and skewness from 60 channels (240 initial features) were reduced by sparse-regression/Lasso feature selection.
entries.condition: Features extracted from imagery EEG; training and test segments were taken from their respective data partitions; random seeds not reported.

entries.text: Compared classifiers were ELM, ELM-L, ELM-R, SVM-R, and LDA; each trial's label was the most frequent output across its 30 segment-level classifications.
entries.condition: EEG imagined-vowel classification; pairwise class combinations; trial-level majority vote over 30 segments; no language model or seeds reported.

entries.text: Evaluation used 10 × 10-fold cross-validation, with results reported for each subject and pairwise classification; no leave-subject-out evaluation is described.
entries.condition: Test set: held-out folds; subjects/speakers: five, reported individually; vocabulary: pairwise combinations of five vowels and mute; decoding/LM: none, 30-segment majority vote; seeds: not reported.

questions.q: What is the proposed decoder and what does it output?
questions.answer: CSP-selected EEG is represented by covariance matrices, mapped to tangent-vector features using a training-set geometric-mean reference, and classified with multiclass mRVM; the output is a prompted class label with a class-membership confidence.

questions.q: Which task results support the paper's performance claims?
questions.answer: The paper reports abstract maxima of 70% for a three-word case and 95% for a two-word case. Table 2 reports group means of 49.0% for vowels, 50.1% for short words, 66.2% for long words, 73.3% for short-versus-long method 1, and 80.1% for method 2; the groups contain different subject subsets.

questions.q: How were the main results evaluated, and what limits generalization?
questions.answer: The paper uses randomized 10-fold within-task trial splits, with 270/30 train/test trials for three-class tasks and 160/40 for two-class tasks. It reports per-subject results rather than a held-out-subject evaluation; random seeds and selection-set handling are not specified.

questions.q: What caveats do the authors acknowledge?
questions.answer: They note non-convex, costly RVM training; computational and covariance-singularity limits of Riemannian features; unstable ELM results; overly restrictive Hurst-based trial rejection; and temporal-correlation inflation under blocked repetition.

questions.q: What does the linked implementation add beyond the paper's method description?
questions.answer: The generic repository scripts expose a randomized fold wrapper and stochastic initializations without explicit seeds, optional training-fold standardization, normalized kernels, and 2-point Gauss-Hermite probability calculation. The manuscript does not identify which repository variant or wrapper generated its results.

questions.q: How do later works on the same dataset compare with tangent+RVM, and do they attribute its accuracy to non-speech factors?
questions.answer: Singh and Gumaste (2019) report ts+ann above copied ts+rvm values (p<0.05 for vowels and short words only); Tates et al. (2026) report median 0.74 under grouped CV vs 0.89 stratified and attribute short-versus-long separation to muscle tension and visual cue.
